vignette: Rohan had been a chaplain at the local hospital for five years when his life took a devastating turn. One fateful evening, while walking home from work, he was brutally mugged by a group of teenagers. They had kicked him repeatedly in the head and chest, leaving him with severe injuries and an even deeper wound - the loss of his wife, who died shortly after the attack due to complications from her own injuries sustained during the struggle. As Rohan struggled to come to terms with the trauma, he found himself increasingly avoidant of crowded places. The mere sight of a large group of people would transport him back to that fateful night, and he could almost smell the metallic scent of his own blood mixed with the sweat of his attackers. He would often catch himself thinking about the event in vivid visual details - the faces of his attackers, the sound of their heavy breathing as they kicked him, the feeling of helplessness as he lay there unable to protect himself or his wife. These memories were not just unpleasant; they also filled Rohan with intense rage. He couldn't shake off the feeling that if only he had been stronger, more vigilant, or more capable, this tragedy could have been averted. This self-blame crept into every aspect of his life, making him wonder if he was somehow responsible for his wife's death. "If I were a better person," he would often think to himself, "this wouldn't have happened." As a chaplain, Rohan had always prided himself on being able to offer solace and guidance to others; now, he felt like he needed it more than anyone. The sound of heavy breathing, in particular, became a potent trigger for Rohan. Whenever he heard someone breathe heavily, whether it was during a crowded elevator ride or a hospital visit, he would be instantly transported back to the scene of the crime. His mind would start racing with thoughts of helplessness and character blame, making him question his own worthiness as a person. He began to avoid hospital visits, opting instead for phone calls or messages, afraid that the sights and sounds of the place where his wife had passed away would trigger another episode. As time went on, Rohan found himself becoming increasingly isolated. His colleagues at the hospital noticed a change in him, but he couldn't bring himself to talk about what was really bothering him. He felt like he was losing control, that the memories and triggers were slowly consuming him whole. The more he tried to avoid them, the more they seemed to seep into every aspect of his life. Rohan's sense of self-worth had taken a beating, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that someone else - anyone else - would have handled things differently. "Why did this happen to me?" he would ask himself, over and over again. The memories of that night continued to haunt him, and with each passing day, the weight of his negative appraisals seemed to grow heavier. It was only when Rohan realized that he couldn't go on living like this - stuck in a cycle of avoidance and self-blame - that he finally sought help. He hoped that therapy would give him a way out of this darkness, a chance to confront the memories and triggers head-on, and perhaps, just perhaps, find some semblance of peace again.
